analysis.problem_summary: Find the third distinct maximum value in an array, returning the absolute maximum if fewer than three distinct values exist.
analysis.intuition: Sorting orders all elements sequentially, placing duplicates adjacent to each other. By sorting in descending order, the maximum element sits at index 0, allowing a simple left-to-right scan to count distinct elements.
approach: Sort the array in ascending order using Java's built-in `Arrays.sort`.
Reverse the array in-place using two pointers to place elements in descending order.
Traverse the array from index 1, tracking the count of unique elements with `eleCount`.
If `eleCount` reaches 3, return `nums[k]`. If the loop finishes without finding 3 distinct maximums, return `nums[0]`.
analysis.why_it_works: Sorting guarantees that identical elements group together and elements appear in decreasing order after reversal. Counting transition points between adjacent elements yields distinct maximums in descending rank.
analysis.key_takeaway: Sorting simplifies k-th distinct value problems by aggregating duplicates and ordering elements, though it incurs an O(n log n) sorting overhead.
analysis.time_explanation: Sorting the array of length `n` takes O(n log n) time. The subsequent reversal and single-pass scan take O(n) time, giving an overall time complexity of O(n log n).
analysis.space_explanation: The array reversal and linear scan are performed in-place using O(1) additional variable space (excluding recursion stack space used by Dual-Pivot Quicksort).

analysis.problem_summary: Find the third distinct maximum value in an array in O(n) time, returning the absolute maximum if fewer than three distinct values exist.
analysis.intuition: Since we only need the top 3 distinct maximums, we do not need to sort the entire array. Maintaining three variables (`max1`, `max2`, `max3`) allows us to update the top 3 distinct numbers on the fly during a single traversal.
approach: Initialize three variables (`max1`, `max2`, `max3`) to `null` (or sentinel values) to track the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd maximums.
If the current number is equal to any of `max1`, `max2`, or `max3`, skip it to ignore duplicates.
If the current number is greater than `max1` (or `max1` is unassigned), cascade values down (`max3 = max2`, `max2 = max1`, `max1 = current`).
Otherwise, if the number is greater than `max2` (or `max2` is unassigned), update `max3 = max2` and `max2 = current`.
Otherwise, if the number is greater than `max3` (or `max3` is unassigned), update `max3 = current`.
After scanning all numbers, return `max3` if it was set; otherwise return `max1`.
analysis.why_it_works: A constant set of 3 variables is sufficient to dynamically maintain the top three distinct elements. Checking for equality before comparison prevents duplicate elements from occupying multiple top positions.
analysis.key_takeaway: When tracking top-k elements for a small, fixed k, using k tracking variables achieves optimal O(n) time and O(1) space without needing heap or sorting operations.
analysis.time_explanation: The algorithm inspects each element in `nums` exactly once and performs a constant number of scalar comparisons and updates, resulting in O(n) total execution time.
analysis.space_explanation: Only three variables are allocated regardless of the input array size, consuming O(1) auxiliary space.
